3099--- ### Assert and Assume
3100-
3101--- Note to developers (Claude):
3102---     The Rocq exercise region extends to End HoareAssertAssume. The
3103---     directive here covers only the initial student tasks because Verso
3104---     cannot compile the whole module as one block.
3105-
3106--- In this exercise, we will extend IMP with two commands, `assert` and
3107--- `assume`. Both commands are ways to indicate that a certain assertion
3108--- should hold any time this part of the program is reached. However they
3109--- differ as follows:
3110-
3111--- - If an `assert` statement fails, it causes the program to go into an error
3112---   state and exit.
3113-
3114--- - If an `assume` statement fails, the program fails to evaluate at all. In
3115---   other words, the program gets stuck and has no final state.
3116-
3117--- The new set of commands is:
3118-
3119-namespace HoareAssertAssume
3120-
3121-inductive Com : Type where
3122-  | skip : Com
3123-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
3124-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
3125-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
3126-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
3127-  | assert : Bexp → Com
3128-  | assume : Bexp → Com
3129-
3130--- Note to developers:
3131---     NOTATION: LATER: Reconsider these precedences
3132-
3133-/-- Imp commands plus `assert` and `assume` -/
3134-declare_syntax_cat haa_com
3135-/-- Assert / assume (`assert (b);`, `assume (b);`).  As with `skip`, the
3136-words `assert` and `assume` are not reserved: the production accepts any
3137-identifier and the macro below rejects everything else. -/
3138-syntax ident " (" imp_bexp ")" ";" : haa_com
3139-
3140-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
3141-syntax ident ";" : haa_com
3142-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
3143-syntax haa_com ppDedent(ppLine haa_com) : haa_com
3144-/-- Assignment -/
3145-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : haa_com
3146-/-- Conditional -/
3147-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : haa_com
3148-/-- Loop -/
3149-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : haa_com
3150-/-- Escape to Lean -/
3151-syntax:max "~" term:max : haa_com
3152-
3153-/-- Include an assert/assume-Imp command in Lean code -/
3154-syntax:min "impa" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
3155-
3156-open Lean in
3157-macro_rules
3158-  | `(impa { $x:ident ; }) =>
3159-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
3160-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
3161-  | `(impa { $h:ident ($b) ; }) =>
3162-    if h.getId == `assert then `(Com.assert (bexp {$b}))
3163-    else if h.getId == `assume then `(Com.assume (bexp {$b}))
3164-    else Macro.throwErrorAt h s!"expected 'assert' or 'assume', got '{h.getId}'"
3165-  | `(impa { $c1 $c2 }) =>
3166-    `(Com.seq (impa {$c1}) (impa {$c2}))
3167-  | `(impa { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
3168-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
3169-  | `(impa { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
3170-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (impa {$c1}) (impa {$c2}))
3171-  | `(impa { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
3172-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (impa {$c}))
3173-  | `(impa { ~$c }) =>
3174-    pure c

3176--- To define the behavior of `assert` and `assume`, we need to add notation
3177--- for an error, which indicates that an assertion has failed. We modify the
3178--- `Com.EvalR` relation, therefore, so that it relates a start state to either
3179--- an end state or to `error`. The `Result` type indicates the end value of a
3180--- program, either a state or an error:
3181-
3182-inductive Result : Type where
3183-  | normal : State → Result
3184-  | error : Result
3185-
3186--- Now we are ready to give you the evaluation relation for the new language.
3187-
3188-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → Result → Prop where
3189-  /- Old rules, several modified -/
3190-  | skip (st : State) :
3191-      EvalR (impa {skip;}) st (.normal st)
3192-  | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
3193-      EvalR (impa {x := ~a;}) st (.normal (x →ₜ n ; st))
3194-  | seqNormal (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' : State) (r : Result)
3195-      (h1 : EvalR c1 st (.normal st')) (h2 : EvalR c2 st' r) :
3196-      EvalR (impa {~c1 ~c2}) st r
3197-  | seqError (c1 c2 : Com) (st : State) (h : EvalR c1 st .error) :
3198-      EvalR (impa {~c1 ~c2}) st .error
3199-  | ifTrue (st : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
3200-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c1 st r) :
3201-      EvalR (impa {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
3202-  | ifFalse (st : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
3203-      (hb : b.eval st = false) (hc : EvalR c2 st r) :
3204-      EvalR (impa {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
3205-  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3206-      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st (.normal st)
3207-  | whileTrueNormal (st st' : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
3208-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st (.normal st'))
3209-      (hloop : EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st' r) :
3210-      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st r
3211-  | whileTrueError (st : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
3212-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st .error) :
3213-      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st .error
3214-  /- Rules for Assert and Assume -/
3215-  | assertTrue (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3216-      EvalR (impa {assert (~b);}) st (.normal st)
3217-  | assertFalse (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3218-      EvalR (impa {assert (~b);}) st .error
3219-  | assume (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3220-      EvalR (impa {assume (~b);}) st (.normal st)
3221-
3222-scoped notation:40 (priority := high) st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " r:41 =>
3223-  Com.EvalR c st0 r
3224-scoped syntax:40 (priority := high) term:41 " =[ " haa_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
3225-scoped macro_rules
3226-  | `($st0 =[ $c:haa_com ]=> $r) => `($st0 =[ impa { $c } ]=> $r)
3227-
3228--- We redefine hoare triples: Now, `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` means that, whenever
3229--- `c` is started in a state satisfying `P`, and terminates with result `r`,
3230--- then `r` is not an error and the state of `r` satisfies `Q`.
3231-
3232-def ValidHoareTriple
3233-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
3234-  ∀ st r,
3235-    (st =[ c ]=> r) → P st →
3236-    (∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q st')
3237-
3238-namespace ValidHoareTriple
3239-
3240-/-- Hoare triple over assert/assume-Imp commands -/
3241-scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " haa_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
3242-
3243-macro_rules
3244-  | `({{ $P }} $c:haa_com {{ $Q }}) =>
3245-      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (impa { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
3246-
3247-end ValidHoareTriple
3248-
3249-open scoped ValidHoareTriple
3250-
3251--- ### Exercise (4 stars): assert_vs_assume ⭐⭐⭐⭐
3252-
3253--- To test your understanding of this modification, give an example
3254--- precondition and postcondition that are satisfied by the `assume` statement
3255--- but not by the `assert` statement.
3256-
3257-theorem assert_assume_differ : ∃ (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion),
3258-    ({{ P }} assume (~b); {{ Q }})
3259-    ∧ ¬ ({{ P }} assert (~b); {{ Q }}) := by
3260-  all_goals
3261-    exists {{ True }}, bexp { false }, ({{ False }} : Assertion)
3262-    constructor
3263-    · unfold ValidHoareTriple
3264-      intro st r hE _
3265-      inversion hE with
3266-      | assume hb => simp at hb
3267-    · intro hC
3268-      unfold ValidHoareTriple at hC
3269-      have h : ∅ =[ assert (false); ]=> Result.error := by
3270-        apply Com.EvalR.assertFalse
3271-        rfl
3272-      obtain ⟨st', heq, _⟩ := hC ∅ Result.error h True.intro
3273-      simp at heq
3274-
3275--- Then prove that any triple for an `assert` also works when `assert` is
3276--- replaced by `assume`.
3277-
3278-theorem assert_implies_assume (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion)
3279-    (hhoare : {{ P }} assert (~b); {{ Q }}) :
3280-    {{ P }} assume (~b); {{ Q }} := by
3281-  all_goals
3282-    unfold ValidHoareTriple
3283-    intro st r hEval hP
3284-    inversion hEval with
3285-    | assume hb =>
3286-      exists st
3287-      have h : st =[ assert (~b); ]=> Result.normal st := by
3288-        apply Com.EvalR.assertTrue
3289-        assumption
3290-      obtain ⟨st', h1, h2⟩ := hhoare st (Result.normal st) h hP
3291-      injection h1 with e
3292-      subst e
3293-      exact ⟨rfl, h2⟩
3294-
3295--- Next, here are proofs for the old hoare rules adapted to the new semantics.
3296--- You don't need to do anything with these.
3297-
3298-theorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
3299-    {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by
3300-  unfold ValidHoareTriple
3301-  intro st r hE hQ
3302-  inversion hE with
3303-  | asgn n h =>
3304-    exists (x →ₜ n ; st)
3305-    subst h
3306-    exact ⟨rfl, hQ⟩
3307-
3308-theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
3309-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
3310-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
3311-  intro st r hc hP
3312-  apply hhoare st r
3313-  · assumption
3314-  · apply himp
3315-    assumption
3316-
3317-theorem hoare_consequence_post (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
3318-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
3319-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
3320-  intro st r hc hP
3321-  unfold ValidHoareTriple at hhoare
3322-  have h : ∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q' st' := by
3323-    apply hhoare st <;> assumption
3324-  obtain ⟨st', hr, hQ'⟩ := h
3325-  exists st'
3326-  constructor
3327-  · assumption
3328-  · apply himp
3329-    assumption
3330-
3331-theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
3332-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{R}}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
3333-    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{R}} := by
3334-  intro st r h12 pre
3335-  inversion h12 with
3336-  | seqNormal st' hc1 hc2 =>
3337-    apply h1
3338-    · apply hc2
3339-    · apply h2 at hc1
3340-      apply hc1 at pre
3341-      obtain ⟨st'', heq, hQ⟩ := pre
3342-      injection heq with e
3343-      subst e
3344-      assumption
3345-  | seqError hc1 =>
3346-    -- Find contradictory assumption
3347-    apply h2 at hc1
3348-    apply hc1 at pre
3349-    obtain ⟨st', hC, _⟩ := pre
3350-    simp at hC
3351-
3352--- Here are the other proof rules (sanity check)
3353-
3354-theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
3355-    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
3356-  intro st r h hP
3357-  inversion h
3358-  exact ⟨st, rfl, hP⟩
3359-
3360-theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
3361-    (hTrue : {{ P ∧ b}} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hFalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b}} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
3362-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
3363-  intro st r hE hP
3364-  inversion hE with
3365-  | ifTrue hb hc =>
3366-    -- b is true
3367-    apply hTrue st r
3368-    · assumption
3369-    · exact ⟨hP, hb⟩
3370-  | ifFalse hb hc =>
3371-    -- b is false
3372-    apply hFalse st r
3373-    · assumption
3374-    · exact ⟨hP, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
3375-
3376-theorem hoare_while (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
3377-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
3378-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{ P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
3379-  intro st r he hP
3380-  have key : ∀ (cmd : Com) (s : State) (r' : Result), (s =[ cmd ]=> r') →
3381-      cmd = (impa { while (~b) { ~c } }) → P s →
3382-      ∃ s', r' = Result.normal s' ∧ P s' ∧ ¬ bassertion b s' := by
3383-    intro cmd s r' hev
3384-    induction hev with
3385-    | whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
3386-        intro heq hp
3387-        injection heq with e1 _
3388-        subst e1
3389-        exact ⟨s0, rfl, hp, bexp_eval_false _ _ hb⟩
3390-    | whileTrueNormal s0 s0' r0 b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
3391-        intro heq hp
3392-        injection heq with e1 e2
3393-        subst e1 e2
3394-        apply ih2 rfl
3395-        obtain ⟨s1, heq1, hp1⟩ := hhoare _ _ hc ⟨hp, hb⟩
3396-        injection heq1 with e
3397-        subst e
3398-        exact hp1
3399-    | whileTrueError s0 b0 c0 hb hc =>
3400-        intro heq hp
3401-        injection heq with e1 e2
3402-        subst e1 e2
3403-        obtain ⟨s1, heq1, _⟩ := hhoare _ _ hc ⟨hp, hb⟩
3404-        simp at heq1
3405-    | skip s0 => intro heq; simp at heq
3406-    | asgn s0 a n x ha => intro heq; simp at heq
3407-    | seqNormal c1 c2 s0 s0' r0 hh1 hh2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp at heq
3408-    | seqError c1 c2 s0 hh ih => intro heq; simp at heq
3409-    | ifTrue s0 r0 b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
3410-    | ifFalse s0 r0 b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
3411-    | assertTrue s0 b0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
3412-    | assertFalse s0 b0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
3413-    | assume s0 b0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
3414-  exact key _ st r he rfl hP
3415-
3416--- Finally, state Hoare rules for `assert` and `assume` and use them to prove
3417--- a simple program correct. Name your rules `hoare_assert` and
3418--- `hoare_assume`.
3419-
3420-/- HIDE: Equivalently, we could make the postcondition Q ∧ b or the
3421-precondition Q → b ... -/
3422-theorem hoare_assert (Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) :
3423-    {{Q ∧ b}} assert (~b); {{ Q }} := by
3424-  intro st r hEval hpre
3425-  obtain ⟨hst, hb⟩ := hpre
3426-  exists st
3427-  inversion hEval with
3428-  | assertTrue hb' => exact ⟨rfl, hst⟩
3429-  | assertFalse hb' => simp [hb'] at hb
3430-
3431-/- Stating this in a backwards-direction friendly way. -/
3432-/- HIDE: Equivalently, we could make the postcondition Q ∧ b... -/
3433-theorem hoare_assume (Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) :
3434-    {{ b → Q }} assume (~b); {{ Q }} := by
3435-  intro st r hEval hst
3436-  exists st
3437-  inversion hEval with
3438-  | assume hb => exact ⟨rfl, hst hb⟩
3439-
3440--- Use your rules to prove the following triple.
3441-
3442-theorem assert_assume_example :
3443-    {{True}}
3444-      assume (X = 1);
3445-      X := X + 1;
3446-      assert (X = 2);
3447-    {{True}} := by
3448-  all_goals
3449-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
3450-    · apply hoare_seq
3451-      · apply hoare_seq
3452-        · apply hoare_assert
3453-        · apply hoare_asgn
3454-      · apply hoare_assume
3455-    · assertion_auto'
3456-
3457-end HoareAssertAssume

7--- # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
8-

21---     to this chapter (and into later files, as appropriate). We haven't done
22---     it yet because it's a shame to complicate the nice simple presentation
23---     here when it's used as the basis for applications like Xavier's static

27---     MWH (port note): The Rocq chapter's "Rocq Automation" tour has been
28---     retooled here for Lean. The tactic combinators `try` and `repeat` (and
29---     the custom-tactic `macro`) are introduced in this chapter; `<;>` and
30---     `simp` were already introduced in Logical Foundations (`<;>` in
31---     `Induction`) so we use them freely and the `<;>` section below is a

35-
36--- In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a tool
37--- to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative programming
38--- language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of conventional
39--- mainstream languages such as C and Java.
40-
41--- Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
42-
43---   Z := X;
44---   Y := 1;
45---   while (Z ≠ 0) {
46---     Y := Y * Z;
47---     Z := Z - 1;
48---   }
49-
50--- We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp; later
51--- in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and introduce
52--- *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative programs.
53-
54--- We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of *arithmetic
55--- and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter, *Slang*; read
56--- that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of arithmetic
57--- expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their evaluation
58--- both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive *relation* (proved
59--- equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program transformation together
60--- with its correctness proof. Those expressions are *variable-free*.
61-
62--- This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
63--- *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
64--- conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
65-
66--- ## Expressions With Variables
67-
68--- Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich our
69--- arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things simple,
70--- we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only hold numbers.
71-
72--- ### States
73-
74--- Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
75--- we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or just
76--- *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some point in
77--- the execution of a program.
78-
79--- For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all* variables,
80--- even though any given program is only able to mention a finite number of
81--- them. Because each variable stores a natural number, we represent the state
82--- as a total map from strings (variable names) to `Nat`, and will use `0` as
83--- the default value in the store.
84-
85--- We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
86--- just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.
87-
88-abbrev Ident := String
89-abbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
90-
91--- ### Syntax
92-
93--- We can add variables to the arithmetic expressions we had before simply by
94--- including one more constructor. (This is a fresh `Aexp`, replacing the
95--- variable-free one from the *Slang* chapter.)
96-
97--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
98---     That should be a live chapter link.
99-
100-inductive Aexp where
101-  | num (n : Nat)
102-  | id (x : Ident)                -- NEW
103-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
104-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
105-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
106-
107--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
108---     Rather than define identifiers as Ident, a more general approach is to
109---     use a **type variable** with `DecidableEq` (as the `Maps` chapter
110---     does), threaded through `Aexp`/`Bexp`/`Com`/`State`. Stashed for a
111---     future decision; the parameterized version would look like:
112---
113---     `inductive Aexp (V : Type) where
114---       | num (n : Nat)
115---       | id (x : V)
116---       | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
117---       | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
118---       | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
119---     -- … then `Bexp V`, `Com V`, `abbrev State (V) [DecidableEq V] :=
120---     -- TotalMap V Nat`, and `[DecidableEq V]` wherever a lookup/update is
121---     -- performed.`
122-
123--- The `Bexp` definition is unchanged, except that it now refers to the new
124--- `Aexp`.
125-
126-inductive Bexp where
127-  | bool (b : Bool)
128-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
129-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
130-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
131-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
132-  | not (b : Bexp)
133-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
134-
135--- Defining a few variable names as shorthands will make examples easier to
136--- read.
137-
138-def W : Ident := "W"
139-def X : Ident := "X"
140-def Y : Ident := "Y"
141-def Z : Ident := "Z"
142-
143--- (This convention for naming program variables (`X`, `Y`, `Z`) clashes a bit
144--- with our earlier use of uppercase letters for types. Since we're not using
145--- polymorphism heavily in the chapters developed to Imp, this overloading
146--- should not cause confusion.)
147-
148--- ### Notations
149-
150--- To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some notations
151--- and implicit coercions.
152-
153--- You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do. Briefly,
154--- though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
155-
156--- - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
157---   grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals further
158---   below.
159-
160--- - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there are
161---   eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`, as
162---   `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for building
163---   larger expressions, with some annotations to define precedence, etc.
164-
165--- - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
166---   `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
167-
168--- Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern exactly,
169--- so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open one if you want
170--- to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.
171-
172-/-- Arithmetic expressions of Imp -/
173-declare_syntax_cat imp_aexp
174-/-- Numeric literal -/
175-syntax:max num : imp_aexp
176-/-- Variable reference -/
177-syntax:max ident : imp_aexp
178-/-- Addition -/
179-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " + " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
180-/-- Subtraction -/
181-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " - " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
182-/-- Multiplication -/
183-syntax:70 imp_aexp:70 " * " imp_aexp:71 : imp_aexp
184-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
185-syntax "(" imp_aexp ")" : imp_aexp
186-/-- Escape to Lean -/
187-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_aexp
188-
189-/-- Embed an Imp arithmetic expression into a Lean term -/
190-syntax:min "aexp " "{" imp_aexp "}" : term
191-
192-open Lean in
193-macro_rules
194-  | `(aexp { $n:num }) => `(Aexp.num $(quote n.getNat))
195-  | `(aexp { $x:ident }) => `(Aexp.id $x)
196-  | `(aexp { ~$e }) => pure e
197-  | `(aexp { $a + $b }) => `(Aexp.plus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
198-  | `(aexp { $a - $b }) => `(Aexp.minus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
199-  | `(aexp { $a * $b }) => `(Aexp.mult (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
200-  | `(aexp { ($a) }) => `(aexp {$a})
201-
202--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: boolean expressions
203-
204-/-- Boolean expressions of Imp -/
205-declare_syntax_cat imp_bexp
206-/-- Boolean literal (`true` or `false`) -/
207-syntax:max ident : imp_bexp
208-/-- Equality of arithmetic expressions -/
209-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " = " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
210-/-- Disequality of arithmetic expressions -/
211-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≠ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
212-/-- Less than or equal -/
213-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≤ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
214-/-- Greater than -/
215-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " > " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
216-/-- Boolean negation -/
217-syntax:70 "¬ " imp_bexp:70 : imp_bexp
218-/-- Boolean conjunction -/
219-syntax:35 imp_bexp:36 " ∧ " imp_bexp:35 : imp_bexp
220-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
221-syntax "(" imp_bexp ")" : imp_bexp
222-/-- Escape to Lean -/
223-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_bexp
224-
225-/-- Embed an Imp boolean expression into a Lean term -/
226-syntax:min "bexp " "{" imp_bexp "}" : term
227-
228--- END DETAILS
229-
230--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: boolean expressions, macro rules
231-
232-open Lean in
233-macro_rules
234-  | `(bexp { $x:ident }) =>
235-    match x.getId with
236-    | `true  => `(Bexp.bool true)
237-    | `false => `(Bexp.bool false)
238-    | _      => Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'true' or 'false', got '{x.getId}'"
239-  | `(bexp { ~$e }) => pure e
240-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp = $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.eq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
241-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≠ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.neq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
242-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≤ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.le (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
243-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp > $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.gt (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
244-  | `(bexp { ¬ $b:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.not (bexp {$b}))
245-  | `(bexp { $b1:imp_bexp ∧ $b2:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.and (bexp {$b1}) (bexp {$b2}))
246-  | `(bexp { ($b:imp_bexp) }) => `(bexp {$b})
247-
248--- END DETAILS
249-
250--- We make it a little easier to write Imp programs using normal constructors
251--- (i.e., without notation), by using *implicit coercions*. In Lean, a `Coe`
252--- instance tells the elaborator how to turn a value of one type into another
253--- automatically:
254-
255--- - `Coe Ident Aexp` lets us write a bare variable (an `Ident`) where an `Aexp`
256---   is expected; the identifier is implicitly wrapped with `id`.
257-
258--- - `OfNat Aexp n` lets us write a numeric literal where an `Aexp` is expected;
259---   it is implicitly wrapped with `num`.
260-
261--- - `Coe Bool Bexp` lets us write a boolean literal (`true`/`false`) where a
262---   `Bexp` is expected; it is implicitly wrapped with `bool`.
263-
264-instance : Coe Ident Aexp where
265-  coe := .id
266-
267-instance (n : Nat) : OfNat Aexp n where
268-  ofNat := .num n
269-
270-instance : Coe Bool Bexp where
271-  coe := .bool
272-
273--- With these coercions we can write `.plus 3 (.mult X 2)` instead of the
274--- fully explicit `.plus (.num 3) (.mult (.id "X") (.num 2))`, and
275--- `.and true (.not …)` instead of `.and (.bool true) (.not …)`. More readably
276--- still, the concrete syntax from the Notations section lets us write these
277--- examples directly:
278-
279-def example_aexp : Aexp := aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
280-def example_bexp : Bexp := bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }
281-
282--- ### Delaborators
283-
284--- The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
285--- `aexp
286--- { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
287--- using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
288--- `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
289--- *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax into a
290--- term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns an
291--- elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output uses our
292--- concrete Imp notation.
293-
294--- Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the matching
295--- piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't recognize is
296--- printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute registers the
297--- top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to display a term headed
298--- by one of those constructors -- unless notation printing has been switched
299--- off with `set_option pp.notation false`, which lets us fall back to the raw
300--- constructors when debugging (see *Desugaring Notations* below). The
301--- companion *category parenthesizer* re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's
302--- precedences demand, so that, e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its
303--- parentheses intact.
304-
305--- You do not need to understand the details, and the code is collapsed below
306--- for that reason. The result is that a `#check`, an `#eval`, or a proof goal
307--- mentioning an Imp expression is displayed in readable Imp syntax rather
308--- than as a pile of constructors.
309-

315-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_aexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
316-@[category_parenthesizer imp_aexp]
317-def imp_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
318-  maybeParenthesize `imp_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
319-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_aexp prec
320-where
321-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do

335-/-- Tag freshly built syntax with the term info that Lean's pretty printer expects. -/
336-def annAsTerm {any} (stx : TSyntax any) : DelabM (TSyntax any) :=
337-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
338-
339-/-- Rebuild `imp_aexp` concrete syntax from an `Aexp` term. -/
340-partial def delabAexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_aexp) := do
341-  let e ← getExpr
342-  let stx ←
343-    match_expr e with
344-    | Aexp.num _ =>
345-      match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
346-      | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
347-      | none   => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
348-    | Aexp.id _ =>
349-      -- A variable reference like aexp { X } elaborates to Aexp.id X where X is the
350-      -- declared Ident constant, so the delaborators print the constant's name as a
351-      -- bare identifier (and also handle the .id "X" string-literal form).
352-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
353-      | .const nm _      => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
354-      | .lit (.strVal s) => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident)
355-      | _                => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
356-    | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
357-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
358-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
359-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
360-    | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
361-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
362-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
363-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
364-    | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
365-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
366-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
367-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
368-    | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← delab))
369-  annAsTerm stx
370-
371-/-- Rebuild `imp_bexp` concrete syntax from a `Bexp` term. -/
372-partial def delabBexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_bexp) := do
373-  let e ← getExpr
374-  let stx ←
375-    match_expr e with
376-    | Bexp.bool _ =>
377-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
378-      | .const ``Bool.true _  => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
379-      | .const ``Bool.false _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
380-      | _                     => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
381-    | Bexp.eq _ _ =>
382-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
383-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
384-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp = $s2:imp_aexp)
385-    | Bexp.neq _ _ =>
386-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
387-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
388-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≠ $s2:imp_aexp)
389-    | Bexp.le _ _ =>
390-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
391-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
392-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≤ $s2:imp_aexp)
393-    | Bexp.gt _ _ =>
394-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
395-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
396-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp > $s2:imp_aexp)
397-    | Bexp.not _ =>
398-      let s ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
399-      `(imp_bexp| ¬ $s)
400-    | Bexp.and _ _ =>
401-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
402-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
403-      `(imp_bexp| $s1 ∧ $s2)
404-    | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← delab))
405-  annAsTerm stx
406-

451--- With these delaborators in place, Lean pretty-prints Imp expressions with
452--- the higher-level notations rather than their raw constructors.

454--- The pretty-printed version of an expression might not exactly match its

463--- ### Evaluation
464-
465--- The arithmetic and boolean evaluators must now be extended to handle
466--- variables, taking a state `st` as an extra argument. A variable is looked
467--- up in the state with the map-indexing notation `st[x]` from the
468--- `Typeclasses` chapter. For the notation to work, we need to
469--- `open scoped MyGetElem`, which opens only the scoped items like notation
470--- from the module.
471-
472-open scoped MyGetElem
473-
474-def Aexp.eval (st : State) (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
475-  match a with
476-  | num   n     =>  n
477-  | id    x     =>  st[x]                    -- NEW
478-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st + a2.eval st
479-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st - a2.eval st
480-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st * a2.eval st
481-
482-def Bexp.eval (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
483-  match b with
484-  | bool b      =>  b
485-  | eq   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st == a2.eval st
486-  | neq  a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st != a2.eval st
487-  | le   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st ≤  a2.eval st
488-  | gt   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st >  a2.eval st
489-  | not  b1     =>  !b1.eval st
490-  | and  b1 b2  =>  b1.eval st && b2.eval st
491-
492-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (st : State) (n : Nat) : (num n).eval st = n := rfl
493-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_id (st : State) (x : Ident) : (Aexp.id x).eval st = st[x] := rfl
494-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
495-    (plus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st + a2.eval st := rfl
496-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
497-    (minus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st - a2.eval st := rfl
498-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
499-    (mult a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st * a2.eval st := rfl
500-
501-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval st = b := rfl
502-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
503-    (eq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st == a2.eval st) := rfl
504-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
505-    (neq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st != a2.eval st) := rfl
506-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
507-    (le a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
508-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
509-    (gt a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st > a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
510-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval st = !b.eval st := rfl
511-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (st : State) (b1 b2 : Bexp) :
512-    (and b1 b2).eval st = (b1.eval st && b2.eval st) := rfl
513-
514--- We reuse the total-map notation (`x →ₜ v ; ∅` etc.) for states.
515-
516-example : aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = 13 := by rfl
517-
518-example : aexp { Z + (X * Y) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; Y →ₜ 4 ; ∅) = 20 := by rfl
519-
520-example : bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = true := by rfl

528--- ## Commands
529-
530--- Now we are ready to define the syntax and behavior of Imp *commands* (or
531--- *statements*). Informally, commands `c` are described by the following BNF
532--- grammar:
533-
534--- c ::= skip
535---     | x := a
536---     | c ; c
537---     | if b then c else c end
538---     | while b do c end
539-
540--- Here is the formal definition of the abstract syntax of commands.
541-
542-inductive Com where
543-  | skip
544-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
545-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com)
546-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
547-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
548-

551-/-- Imp commands -/
552-declare_syntax_cat imp_com
553-
554--- END DETAILS

556--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: commands, macro rules
557-
558-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
559-syntax ident ";" : imp_com
560-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
561-syntax imp_com ppDedent(ppLine imp_com) : imp_com
562-/-- Assignment -/
563-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : imp_com
564-/-- Conditional -/
565-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
566-/-- Loop -/
567-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
568-/-- Escape to Lean -/
569-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_com
570-
571-/-- Include an Imp command in Lean code -/
572-syntax:min "imp" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
573-
574-open Lean in
575-macro_rules
576-  | `(imp { $x:ident ; }) =>
577-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
578-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
579-  | `(imp { $c1 $c2 }) =>
580-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
581-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
582-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
583-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
584-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
585-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
586-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
587-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
588-    pure c
589-

592--- Just as we did for expressions, we add a delaborator so that Lean prints
593--- commands back in the `imp { … }` concrete syntax (see the Delaborators
594--- section above). It reuses the expression delaborators for the condition of
595--- an `if`/`while` and for the right-hand side of an assignment, and prints an
596--- unrecognized subcommand with the `~` escape.
597-

600-namespace Imp.Delab
601-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
602-
603-/-- Rebuild `imp_com` concrete syntax from a `Com` term. -/
604-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) := do
605-  let e ← getExpr
606-  let stx ←
607-    match_expr e with
608-    -- `mkIdent` rather than a quotation-literal `skip`, which would pick up
609-    -- macro hygiene scopes and print as `skip✝`.
610-    | Com.skip => `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `skip):ident ;)
611-    | Com.asgn _ _ =>
612-      match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
613-      | .const nm _ =>
614-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
615-        `(imp_com| $(mkIdent nm):ident := $a;)
616-      | .lit (.strVal s) =>
617-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
618-        `(imp_com| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident := $a;)
619-      | _ => `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
620-    | Com.seq _ _ =>
621-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabComInner
622-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabComInner
623-      `(imp_com| $s1 $s2)
624-    | Com.cond _ _ _ =>
625-      let b  ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
626-      let c1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabComInner
627-      let c2 ← withAppArg delabComInner
628-      `(imp_com| if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2})
629-    | Com.whileDo _ _ =>
630-      let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
631-      let c ← withAppArg delabComInner
632-      `(imp_com| while ($b) {$c})
633-    | _ => `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
634-  annAsTerm stx
635-
636-@[delab app.Com.skip, delab app.Com.asgn, delab app.Com.seq,
637-  delab app.Com.cond, delab app.Com.whileDo]
638-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
639-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
640-    | Com.skip => true
641-    | Com.asgn _ _ => true
642-    | Com.seq _ _ => true
643-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
644-    | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
645-    | _ => false
646-  match ← delabComInner with
647-  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
648-  | e => `(term| imp { $e })
649-
650-end Imp.Delab

654--- As an example, here is the factorial function again, written as a formal
655--- definition. When this command terminates, the variable `Y` will contain the
656--- factorial of the initial value of `X`. (Compare this to the concrete Imp
657--- program at the very start of the chapter.)
658-
659-def fact_in_lean : Com := imp {
660-  Z := X;
661-  Y := 1;
662-  while (Z ≠ 0) {
663-    Y := Y * Z;
664-    Z := Z - 1;
665-  }
666-}
667-
668--- Because we registered a delaborator, we can inspect a defined program with
669--- `#print`, which pretty prints the stored definition using the same syntax:
670-
671-/--
672-info: def fact_in_lean : Com :=
673-imp {
674-  Z := X;
675-  Y := 1;
676-  while (Z ≠ 0) {
677-    Y := Y * Z;
678-    Z := Z - 1;
679-  }
680-}
681--/
682-#guard_msgs in
683-#print fact_in_lean
684-
685--- ### Desugaring Notations
686-
687--- The `imp { … }` notation, together with the delaborators, is purely a
688--- convenience for reading and writing programs. Occasionally, such as when
689--- debugging a definition or a stuck proof, the concrete syntax `hide`s the
690--- underlying structure we want to see. For those moments we can switch the
691--- Imp notation off in Lean's output with `set_option pp.notation false`,
692--- which our delaborators honor.
693-
694--- Note that unlike a `def`, `imp { … }` is a `macro` which is expanded during
695--- elaboration, **before** the resulting term is type-checked. So
696--- `fact_in_lean` is not a program hidden behind a layer of notation that a
697--- proof must first peel back; it simply **is** the underlying tree of `Com`,
698--- `Aexp`, and `Bexp` constructors. Consequently, when a proof goal mentions
699--- an Imp program, tactics such as `cases`, `injection`, and `simp` already
700--- act on those constructors directly -- there is nothing to "unfold". The
701--- delaborators affect only how that tree is **displayed**. Nevertheless,
702--- seeing the raw constructors is sometimes very helpful!
703-
704-#check imp { X := X + 1; }
705-
706-set_option pp.notation false in
707-#check imp { X := X + 1; }
708-

710-

712-
713--- Assignment:
714-
715-def plus2 : Com := imp { X := X + 2; }
716-def XtimesYinZ : Com := imp { Z := X * Y; }

718--- Loops:
719-

721-  Z := Z - 1;
722-  X := X - 1;
723-}

726-  while (X ≠ 0) {
727-    ~subtract_slowly_body
728-  }
729-}

731-def subtract_3_from_5_slowly : Com := imp {
732-  X := 3;
733-  Z := 5;
734-  ~subtract_slowly
735-}

738-
739-def loop : Com := imp { while (true) { skip; } }

741--- ## Evaluating Commands
742-
743--- Next we need to define what it means to evaluate an Imp command. The fact
744--- that `while` loops don't necessarily terminate makes defining an evaluation
745--- function tricky.
746-
747--- ### Evaluation as a Function (Failed Attempt)
748-
749--- Here's an attempt at defining an evaluation function for commands (with a
750--- bogus `while` case).
751-
752-def Com.ceval_fun_no_while (st : State) (c : Com) : State :=
753-  match c with
754-  | imp {skip;} => st
755-  | imp {x := ~a;} => (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
756-  | imp {~c1 ~c2} =>
757-      let st' := ceval_fun_no_while st c1
758-      ceval_fun_no_while st' c2
759-  | imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}} =>
760-      if b.eval st then ceval_fun_no_while st c1
761-      else ceval_fun_no_while st c2
762-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => st     -- bogus
763-
764--- In a more conventional functional language like OCaml or Haskell we could
765--- add the `while` case as follows:
766-
767--- | .whileDo b c =>
768---     if b.eval st then ceval_fun st (.seq c (.whileDo b c))
769---     else st
770-
771--- Lean doesn't accept such a definition ("fail to show termination") because
772--- the function we want to define is not guaranteed to terminate. Indeed, it
773--- *doesn't* always terminate: the full `ceval_fun` applied to the `loop`
774--- program above would run forever. Since Lean aims to be not just a
775--- programming language but also a consistent logic, any potentially
776--- non-terminating function must be rejected. Here is what would go wrong if
777--- Lean allowed non-terminating recursive functions:
778-
779--- def loop_false (n : Nat) : False := loop_false n
780-
781--- That is, propositions like `False` would become provable (`loop_false 0`
782--- would be a proof of `False`), a disaster for logical consistency.
783-
784--- Thus, because it doesn't terminate on all inputs, the full `ceval_fun`
785--- cannot be written in Lean -- at least not without additional tricks and
786--- workarounds.
787-
788--- Note to developers:
789---     Perhaps that discussion should be moved to -- or previewed in --
790---     Logic.v? MRC'20: It's already in ProofObjects (which not everyone
791---     sees).
792-
793--- ### Evaluation as a Relation
794-
795--- Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather than a
796--- *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather than a `State`, similar
797--- to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR` above.
798-
799--- This is an important change. Besides freeing us from awkward workarounds,
800--- it gives us more flexibility in the definition. For example, if we add
801--- nondeterministic features like `any` to the language, we want the
802--- definition of evaluation to be nondeterministic -- i.e., not only will it
803--- not be total, it will not even be a function!
804-
805--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
806---     I kind of hate this notation. Is there something more standard in Lean?
807---     CSLib precedent maybe?
808-
809--- We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR` relation:
810--- `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c` in a starting state `st`
811--- results in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c` takes state
812--- `st` to `st'`".
813-
814--- Operational Semantics
815-
816--- Note to developers (before next release):
817---     BCP 21: I wonder if `seq` would be easier to work with if st' and st''
818---     were swapped...
819-
820--- Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as inference rules
821--- for readability:
822-
823---                         -----------------                  (skip)
824---                         st =[ skip ]=> st

876-  | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
877-      (hc : EvalR c st st') (hloop : Com.EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st' st'') :

981--- ### Determinism of Evaluation
982-
983--- Changing from a computational to a relational definition of evaluation is a
984--- good move because it frees us from the artificial requirement that
985--- evaluation be a total function. But it raises a question: is the relational
986--- definition really a partial *function*? Could the same command, from the
987--- same state, evaluate to two different final states? In fact this cannot
988--- happen: `ceval` *is* a partial function.
989-
990-theorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st1 st2 : State)
991-    (e1 : st =[ c ]=> st1) (e2 : st =[ c ]=> st2) : st1 = st2 := by
992-  induction e1 generalizing st2 with
993-  | skip st =>
994-      cases e2 with
995-      | skip => rfl
996-  | asgn st a n x h =>
997-      cases e2 with
998-      | asgn _ _ n' _ h' => subst h; subst h'; rfl
999-  | seq c1 c2 st st' st'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1000-      cases e2 with
1001-      | seq _ _ _ st2' _ h1' h2' =>
1002-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ h1'
1003-          subst hst
1004-          exact ih2 _ h2'
1005-  | ifTrue st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
1006-      cases e2 with
1007-      | ifTrue _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
1008-      | ifFalse _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => simp_all
1009-  | ifFalse st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
1010-      cases e2 with
1011-      | ifTrue _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => simp_all
1012-      | ifFalse _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
1013-  | whileFalse b st c hb =>
1014-      cases e2 with
1015-      | whileFalse _ _ _ hb' => rfl
1016-      | whileTrue _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' hl' => simp_all
1017-  | whileTrue st st' st'' b c hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1018-      cases e2 with
1019-      | whileFalse _ _ _ hb' => simp_all
1020-      | whileTrue _ st2' _ _ _ hb' hc' hl' =>
1021-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ hc'
1022-          subst hst
1023-          exact ih2 _ hl'
1024-
1025--- ### Exercise (3 stars): pup_to_n ⭐⭐⭐
1026-
1027--- Write an Imp program that sums the numbers from `1` to `X` (inclusive) in
1028--- the variable `Y`. Your program should update the state as shown in
1029--- `pup_to_2_ceval`, which you can reverse-engineer to discover the program
1030--- you should write. The proof of that theorem will be somewhat lengthy.
1031-
1032-def pup_to_n : Com := (
1033-  imp {
1034-    Y := 0;
1035-    while (1 ≤ X) {
1036-      Y := Y + X;
1037-      X := X - 1;
1038-    }
1039-  })
1040-
1041-theorem pup_to_2_ceval :
1042-    (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) =[ pup_to_n ]=>
1043-      (X →ₜ 0 ; Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
1044-  all_goals
1045-    unfold pup_to_n
1046-    apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
1047-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1048-    · apply Com.EvalR.whileTrue (st' := (X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
1049-      · rfl
1050-      · apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅)) <;>
1051-          (apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl)
1052-      · apply Com.EvalR.whileTrue
1053-          (st' := (X →ₜ 0 ; Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
1054-        · rfl
1055-        · apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅)) <;>
1056-            (apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl)
1057-        · apply Com.EvalR.whileFalse; rfl

1059--- ## Reasoning About Imp Programs
1060-
1061--- We'll get into more systematic and powerful techniques for reasoning about
1062--- Imp programs in the next chapter, but we can already do a few things
1063--- (albeit in a somewhat low-level way) just by working with the bare
1064--- definitions. This section explores some examples.
1065-
1066-theorem plus2_spec (st : State) (n : Nat) (st' : State)
1067-    (hx : st[X] = n) (heval : st =[ plus2 ]=> st') :
1068-    st'[X] = n + 2 := by
1069-  -- Inverting `heval` forces one step of the `ceval` computation: since
1070-  -- `plus2` is an assignment, `st'` must be `st` extended at `X`.
1071-  unfold plus2 at heval
1072-  cases heval with
1073-  | asgn _ _ m _ h =>
1074-      simp only [Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num] at h
1075-      rw [TotalMap.update_eq]
1076-      lia
1077-
1078--- ### Exercise (3 stars): XtimesYinZ_spec ⭐⭐⭐

1080--- State and prove a specification of `XtimesYinZ`.

1082-/- Here is a specification in the style of `plus2_spec`: -/
1083-theorem XtimesYinZ_spec1 (st : State) (nx ny : Nat) (st' : State)
1084-    (hx : st[X] = nx) (hy : st[Y] = ny) (heval : st =[ XtimesYinZ ]=> st') :
1085-    st'[Z] = nx * ny := by
1086-  unfold XtimesYinZ at heval
1087-  cases heval with
1088-  | asgn _ _ n _ h =>
1089-      simp only [Aexp.eval_mult, Aexp.eval_id] at h
1090-      subst hx hy
1091-      rw [TotalMap.update_eq]
1092-      exact h.symm
1093-

1095-theorem XtimesYinZ_spec (st : State) :
1096-    st =[ XtimesYinZ ]=> (Z →ₜ st[X] * st[Y] ; st) := by
1097-  unfold XtimesYinZ
1098-  apply Com.EvalR.asgn
1099-  rfl
1100-

1103-  exact ⟨(Z →ₜ st[X] * st[Y] ; st), by unfold XtimesYinZ; apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl⟩

1105--- ### Exercise (3 stars): loop_never_stops ⭐⭐⭐
1106-
1107--- Hint: proceed by induction on the assumed derivation showing that `loop`
1108--- terminates. Most of the cases are immediately contradictory and so can be
1109--- solved in one step (by `simp`/`discriminate` on the impossible command
1110--- equation).
1111-
1112-theorem loop_never_stops (st st' : State) : ¬ (st =[ loop ]=> st') := by
1113-  all_goals
1114-    intro contra
1115-    -- Generalize over the command so the induction remembers what `loop` is.
1116-    have key : ∀ (c : Com) (s s' : State), (s =[ c ]=> s') → c = loop → False := by
1117-      intro c s s' hce
1118-      induction hce with
1119-      | whileFalse b s0 c0 hb =>
1120-          intro heq; unfold loop at heq; injection heq with e1 _
1121-          subst e1; simp at hb
1122-      | whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1123-          intro heq; exact ih2 heq
1124-      | skip s0 => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1125-      | asgn s0 a n x h => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1126-      | seq c1 c2 s0 s0' s0'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1127-      | ifTrue s0 s0' b c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1128-      | ifFalse s0 s0' b c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1129-    exact key loop st st' contra rfl

1131--- ### Exercise (3 stars): no_whiles_eqv ⭐⭐⭐
1132-
1133--- The following function yields `true` just on programs with no while loops.
1134--- Using `inductive`, write a property `Com.NoWhilesR` that holds exactly when
1135--- `c` is while-free, then prove it equivalent to `Com.no_whiles`.
1136-
1137-def Com.no_whiles (c : Com) : Bool :=
1138-  match c with
1139-  | imp {skip;} => true
1140-  | imp {_x := ~_a;} => true
1141-  | imp {~c1 ~c2} => no_whiles c1 && no_whiles c2
1142-  | imp {if (~_) {~ct} else {~cf}} => no_whiles ct && no_whiles cf
1143-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => false
1144-
1145-inductive Com.NoWhilesR : Com → Prop where
1146-  | skip : Com.NoWhilesR (imp { skip; })
1147-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) : Com.NoWhilesR (imp { x := ~a; })
1148-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (h1 : Com.NoWhilesR c1) (h2 : Com.NoWhilesR c2) :
1149-      Com.NoWhilesR (imp { ~c1 ~c2 })
1150-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (h1 : Com.NoWhilesR c1) (h2 : Com.NoWhilesR c2) :
1151-      Com.NoWhilesR (imp { if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } })
1152-
1153-theorem no_whiles_eqv (c : Com) : c.no_whiles = true ↔ Com.NoWhilesR c := by
1154-  all_goals
1155-    constructor
1156-    · induction c with
1157-      | skip => intro _; exact .skip
1158-      | asgn x a => intro _; exact .asgn x a
1159-      | seq c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1160-          intro h; simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at h
1161-          exact .seq _ _ (ih1 h.1) (ih2 h.2)
1162-      | cond b c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1163-          intro h; simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at h
1164-          exact .cond _ _ _ (ih1 h.1) (ih2 h.2)
1165-      | whileDo b c ih => intro h; simp [Com.no_whiles] at h
1166-    · intro h
1167-      induction h with
1168-      | skip => rfl
1169-      | asgn x a => rfl
1170-      | seq c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp [Com.no_whiles, ih1, ih2]
1171-      | cond b c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp [Com.no_whiles, ih1, ih2]
1172-
1173--- ### Exercise (4 stars): no_whiles_terminating ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1174-
1175--- Imp programs that don't involve while loops always terminate. State and
1176--- prove a theorem `no_whiles_terminating` that says this. Use either
1177--- `Com.no_whiles` or `Com.NoWhilesR`, as you prefer.
1178-
1179-theorem no_whiles_terminating (c : Com) (st : State) (h : Com.NoWhilesR c) :
1180-    ∃ st', st =[ c ]=> st' := by
1181-  all_goals
1182-    induction h generalizing st with
1183-    | skip => exact ⟨st, .skip st⟩
1184-    | asgn x a => exact ⟨(x →ₜ a.eval st ; st), .asgn st a (a.eval st) x rfl⟩
1185-    | seq c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1186-        obtain ⟨st', hc1⟩ := ih1 st
1187-        obtain ⟨st'', hc2⟩ := ih2 st'
1188-        exact ⟨st'', .seq c1 c2 st st' st'' hc1 hc2⟩
1189-    | cond b c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1190-        cases hb : b.eval st with
1191-        | true =>
1192-            obtain ⟨st', hc1⟩ := ih1 st
1193-            exact ⟨st', .ifTrue st st' b c1 c2 hb hc1⟩
1194-        | false =>
1195-            obtain ⟨st', hc2⟩ := ih2 st
1196-            exact ⟨st', .ifFalse st st' b c1 c2 hb hc2⟩
1197-
1198--- And here is an alternative solution by induction on `c` (using
1199--- `Com.no_whiles` instead of `Com.NoWhilesR`):
1200-
1201-theorem no_whiles_terminating' (c : Com) (st1 : State)
1202-    (hb : c.no_whiles = true) : ∃ st2, st1 =[ c ]=> st2 := by
1203-  induction c generalizing st1 with
1204-  | skip => exact ⟨st1, .skip st1⟩
1205-  | asgn x a => exact ⟨(x →ₜ a.eval st1 ; st1), .asgn st1 a (a.eval st1) x rfl⟩
1206-  | seq c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1207-      simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at hb
1208-      obtain ⟨st1', hc1⟩ := ih1 st1 hb.1
1209-      obtain ⟨st1'', hc2⟩ := ih2 st1' hb.2
1210-      exact ⟨st1'', .seq c1 c2 st1 st1' st1'' hc1 hc2⟩
1211-  | cond b ct cf ih1 ih2 =>
1212-      simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at hb
1213-      cases hbev : b.eval st1 with
1214-      | true =>
1215-          obtain ⟨st2, h⟩ := ih1 st1 hb.1
1216-          exact ⟨st2, .ifTrue st1 st2 b ct cf hbev h⟩
1217-      | false =>
1218-          obtain ⟨st2, h⟩ := ih2 st1 hb.2
1219-          exact ⟨st2, .ifFalse st1 st2 b ct cf hbev h⟩
1220-  | whileDo b c ih => simp [Com.no_whiles] at hb

6--- Hoare Logic, covering axiomatic semantics, program verification, and
7--- reasoning about imperative programs. Please check back later!

12--- follows:
13-

15--- author       =   {Mike Hicks and Benjamin C. Pierce and the SF-in-Lean team},
16--- title        =   "Hoare Logic",

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
4-
5-namespace SLFCommand
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-
9-meta section
10-
11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
186-

HL/Slang.lean

1-import HL.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---     We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7---     proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8---     width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9-
10--- We begin by looking at a language we call **Slang** (for *simple
11--- language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets us introduce key concepts
12--- for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics* of programming languages and
13--- show how those concepts are realized in Lean.
14-
15--- (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
16--- Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked through
17--- it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next chapter of
18--- this one.)
19-
20--- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
21-
22--- Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
23--- sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
24-
25--- ### Syntax
26-
27-namespace Slang
28-
29--- These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
30--- boolean expressions.
31-
32-inductive Aexp where
33-  | num (n : Nat)
34-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
35-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
36-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
37-
38-inductive Bexp where
39-  | bool (b : Bool)
40-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
41-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
42-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
43-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
44-  | not (b : Bexp)
45-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
46-
47--- In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete syntax*
48--- that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax trees --
49--- the process that, for example, would translate the string `"1 + 2 * 3"` to
50--- the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
51-
52--- For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
53--- defining the same abstract syntax:
54-
55--- a ::= nat
56---     | a + a
57---     | a − a
58---     | a * a
59--- b ::= bool
60---     | a = a
61---     | a ≠ a
62---     | a ≤ a
63---     | a > a
64---     | ¬ b
65---     | b ∧ b
66-
67--- Compared to the Lean version above...
68-
69--- - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions about
70---   the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the addition
71---   operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other aspects of
72---   lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence of `+`, `-`, and
73---   `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions, etc.) unspecified. Some
74---   additional information -- and human intelligence -- would be required to
75---   turn this description into a formal definition, e.g., for implementing a
76---   compiler. The Lean version consistently omits all this information and
77---   concentrates on the abstract syntax only.
78-
79--- - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its informality
80---   makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like discussions at the
81---   blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more important than nailing
82---   down every detail precisely.
83-
84---   Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch freely
85---   among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of BNF they're
86---   using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready informal
87---   understanding is all that's important.
88-
89--- It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones for
90--- communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
91--- implementations and proofs.
92-
93--- ### Evaluation
94-
95--- *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
96-
97-def Aexp.eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
98-  match a with
99-  | num   n     =>  n
100-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval + a2.eval
101-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval - a2.eval
102-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval * a2.eval
103-
104--- By convention, we pair the definition with one *simplification lemma* per
105--- constructor, specifying how `eval` behaves on that constructor. Proofs then
106--- rewrite by these lemmas rather than peeking through the definition of
107--- `eval`. We tag each lemma `@[simp]`, so `simp` applies them automatically.
108-
109-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
110-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (plus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval + a2.eval := rfl
111-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (minus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval - a2.eval := rfl
112-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (mult a1 a2).eval = a1.eval * a2.eval := rfl
113-
114-example : Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
115-
116--- Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean, and we give it
117--- the same treatment.
118-
119-def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
120-  match b with
121-  | bool b     =>  b
122-  | eq   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval == a2.eval
123-  | neq  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval != a2.eval
124-  | le   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval ≤ a2.eval
125-  | gt   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval > a2.eval
126-  | not  b1    =>  !eval b1
127-  | and  b1 b2 =>  eval b1 && eval b2
128-
129-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
130-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (eq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval == a2.eval) := rfl
131-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (neq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval != a2.eval) := rfl
132-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (le a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval ≤ a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
133-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (gt a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval > a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
134-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
135-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (b1 b2 : Bexp) : (and b1 b2).eval = (b1.eval && b2.eval) := rfl
136-
137--- It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
138--- `a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval` returns a
139--- `Bool` so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide` coercion. You can observe the
140--- call to `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and `Bexp.eval_gt`.
141-
142--- _Quiz:_
143-
144--- What does the following expression evaluate to?
145-
146--- Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
147-
148--- (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
149-
150--- ### Optimization
151-
152--- We can now start to get some mileage out of these definitions. Suppose we
153--- define a function that takes an arithmetic expression and slightly
154--- simplifies it, changing every occurrence of `0 + e` (i.e.,
155--- `.plus (.num 0) e`) into just `e`.
156-
157-def Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
158-  match a with
159-  | num   n          => num n
160-  | plus  (num 0) e2 => optimize0plus e2
161-  | plus  e1      e2 => plus  (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
162-  | minus e1      e2 => minus (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
163-  | mult  e1      e2 => mult  (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
164-
165--- To gain confidence that our optimization is doing the right thing we can
166--- test it on some examples and see if the output looks OK.
167-
168-example :
169-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
170-                               (.plus (.num 0)
171-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
172-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
173-
174--- But if we want to be certain the optimization is correct -- that evaluating
175--- an optimized expression *always* gives the same result as the original --
176--- we should prove it!
177-
178--- Here is a first, deliberately explicit, proof, by induction on `a`. The
179--- interesting case is `plus`: because `optimize0plus` treats `plus (num 0) e`
180--- specially, we case-split on the left operand `a1` -- and, when it is a
181--- numeral, on whether that numeral is `0` -- to line the proof up with the
182--- function's own branches. Once the constructors are exposed, each case is
183--- discharged by essentially the same incantation: unfold `optimize0plus`,
184--- rewrite `eval` by its characterizing lemmas, then finish with the induction
185--- hypotheses. Notice how repetitive that makes the proof.
186-
187-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
188-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
189-  induction a with
190-  | num n => rfl
191-  | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
192-    cases a1 with
193-    | num n =>
194-      cases n with
195-      | zero =>
196-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
197-        exact ih2
198-      | succ n =>
199-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
200-        rw [ih2]
201-    | plus b1 b2 =>
202-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
203-      rw [ih1, ih2]
204-    | minus b1 b2 =>
205-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
206-      rw [ih1, ih2]
207-    | mult b1 b2 =>
208-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
209-      rw [ih1, ih2]
210-  | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
211-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
212-    rw [ih1, ih2]
213-  | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
214-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
215-    rw [ih1, ih2]
216-
217--- We can do much better. The case analysis we performed by hand -- peeling
218--- `plus` apart to reach the `plus (num 0) e` branch -- is exactly the case
219--- analysis that `optimize0plus` itself performs. The `fun_induction` tactic
220--- inducts along a function's **own** recursion structure:
221--- `fun_induction
222--- Aexp.optimize0plus a` hands us one goal per branch of
223--- `optimize0plus` -- the special `plus (num 0) e` branch included -- so the
224--- nested `cases` disappear.
225-
226--- Every remaining goal now has the same shape, so we can attack them
227--- uniformly with the `<;>` combinator, which runs a single tactic on **all**
228--- the goals produced by the induction. That single tactic is `simp_all`: it
229--- rewrites `eval` by the `@[simp]` characterizing lemmas and uses the
230--- induction hypotheses -- which `simp_all` picks up from the local context
231--- automatically -- to close each goal. The whole proof collapses to two
232--- lines.
233-
234-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
235-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
236-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
237-
238--- ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
239-
240--- Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change the value of
241--- an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all the `Aexp`s that appear in
242--- a `Bexp` without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a function that
243--- performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it sound. Use the
244--- combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short and elegant as
245--- possible.
246-
247-def Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := (
248-  match b with
249-  | bool b    =>  bool b
250-  | eq a1 a2  =>  eq a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
251-  | neq a1 a2 =>  neq a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
252-  | le a1 a2  =>  le a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
253-  | gt a1 a2  =>  gt a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
254-  | not b1    =>  not (optimize0plusB b1)
255-  | and b1 b2 =>  and (optimize0plusB b1) (optimize0plusB b2))
256-
257-theorem optimize0plusB_test1 :
258-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
259-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
260-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := (by rfl)
261-
262-theorem optimize0plusB_test2 :
263-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
264-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
265-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := (by rfl)
266-
267-theorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
268-    b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
269-  all_goals
270-    induction b <;>
271-      simp_all [Bexp.optimize0plusB, optimize0plus_sound]
272-
273--- ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize ⭐⭐⭐⭐
274-
275--- The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is only one of
276--- many possible optimizations on arithmetic and boolean expressions. Write a
277--- more sophisticated optimizer and prove it correct. (You will probably find
278--- it easiest to start small -- add just a single, simple optimization and its
279--- correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to something more
280--- interesting.)
281-
282--- ## Evaluation as a Relation
283-
284--- We have presented `Aexp.eval` and `Bexp.eval` as functions defined by
285--- recursion. Another way to think about evaluation -- one that is often more
286--- flexible -- is as a *relation* between expressions and their values. This
287--- perspective leads to inductive definitions like the following.
288-
289-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
290-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
291-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
292-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
293-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
294-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
295-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
296-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
297-
298--- One comment on the style of this definition. We could instead have
299--- presented this relation with **positional** hypotheses -- no names for the
300--- premises.
301-
302-namespace ArithUnnamed
303-
304-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
305-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
306-  | plus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.plus e1 e2) (n1 + n2)
307-  | minus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.minus e1 e2) (n1 - n2)
308-  | mult (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.mult e1 e2) (n1 * n2)
309-
310-end ArithUnnamed
311-
312--- The version above makes the rules somewhat easier to read, but gives less
313--- control over naming the hypotheses during proofs involving the relation.
314--- For this reason we adopt the named style.
315-
316--- It will be convenient to have an infix notation for `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll
317--- write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value
318--- `n`.
319-
320-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => Aexp.EvalR e n
321-
322--- In Lean the `notation` is declared right after the inductive. The `scoped`
323--- keyword allows us to scope the notation to the present namespace so it
324--- doesn't collide with other evaluation relations later.

332--- ### Inference Rule Notation
333-
334--- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
335--- `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form of
336--- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
337--- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like
338--- this as an inference rule:
339-
340--- e1 ⇓ n1
341---                          e2 ⇓ n2
342---                     ------------------          (plus)
343---                     plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
344-
345--- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
346--- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
347-
348--- | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) :
349---         EvalR a1 n1 →
350---         EvalR a2 n2 →
351---         EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
352-
353--- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
354--- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
355--- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
356--- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
357--- variables mentioned in the rule (`e1`, `n1`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
358--- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
359--- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
360--- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
361--- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
362--- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
363--- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
364--- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
365-
366--- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
367--- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
368--- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
369--- `e1` and `n1` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
370--- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:
371-
372--- ---------                (num)
373---                         num n ⇓ n
374-
375---                          e1 ⇓ n1
376---                          e2 ⇓ n2
377---                     ------------------           (plus)
378---                     plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
379-
380---                          e1 ⇓ n1
381---                          e2 ⇓ n2
382---                    -------------------           (minus)
383---                    minus e1 e2 ⇓ n1-n2
384-
385---                          e1 ⇓ n1
386---                          e2 ⇓ n2
387---                     ------------------           (mult)
388---                     mult e1 e2 ⇓ n1*n2
389-

395--- Which rules are needed to prove the following?
396-
397--- .mult (.plus (.num 3) (.num 1)) (.num 0) ⇓ 0
398-
399--- (A) `num` and `plus` (B) `num` only (C) `num` and `mult` (D) `mult` and
400--- `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`
