412--- ### Exercise (1 star): beval_rules ⭐
413-
414--- Here, again, is the definition of the `Bexp.eval` function:
415-
416--- def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
417---   match b with
418---   | bool b     => b
419---   | eq   a1 a2 => a1.eval == a2.eval
420---   | neq  a1 a2 => a1.eval != a2.eval
421---   | le   a1 a2 => a1.eval ≤ a2.eval
422---   | gt   a1 a2 => a1.eval > a2.eval
423---   | not  b1    => !eval b1
424---   | and  b1 b2 => eval b1 && eval b2
425-
426--- Write out a corresponding definition of boolean evaluation as a relation
427--- (in inference rule notation).
428-
429--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
430---     Don't understand the parenthetical comment here.
431-
432--- Answer (`⇓b` is defined below):
433-
434---                         -----------              (bool)
435---                         bool b ⇓b b
436-
437---                         e1 ⇓ n1
438---                         e2 ⇓ n2
439---                    ----------------------        (eq)
440---                    eq e1 e2 ⇓b (n1 =? n2)
441-
442---                         e1 ⇓ n1
443---                         e2 ⇓ n2
444---                  ----------------------------    (neq)
445---                  neq e1 e2 ⇓b negb (n1 =? n2)
446-
447---                         e1 ⇓ n1
448---                         e2 ⇓ n2
449---                    -----------------------       (le)
450---                    le e1 e2 ⇓b (n1 <=? n2)
451-
452---                         e1 ⇓ n1
453---                         e2 ⇓ n2
454---                 ----------------------------     (gt)
455---                 gt e1 e2 ⇓b negb (n1 <=? n2)
456-
457---                           e ⇓b b
458---                       ---------------            (not)
459---                       not e ⇓b negb b
460-
461---                         e1 ⇓b b1
462---                         e2 ⇓b b2
463---                   -----------------------        (and)
464---                   and e1 e2 ⇓b andb b1 b2

466--- ### Equivalence of the Definitions
467-
468--- It is straightforward to prove that the relational and functional
469--- definitions of evaluation agree.
470-
471-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
472-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
473-  constructor
474-  · intro h
475-    induction h with
476-    | num n => rfl
477-    | plus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
478-    | minus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
479-    | mult a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih1, ih2]
480-  · intro h
481-    subst h
482-    induction a with
483-    | num n => exact .num n
484-    | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .plus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
485-    | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .minus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
486-    | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .mult a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
487-
488--- We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more automation like we did
489--- in the previous section.
490-
491--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
492---     the `workinclass!` marker should signal this live in-class exercise.
493---     But it is not rendering properly on the HTML. In fact it replaces
494---     `workinclass!` with the `all_goals` tactic, which we don't need.
495-
496-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
497-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
498-  all_goals
499-    constructor
500-    · intro h; induction h <;> simp_all
501-    · intro h; subst h; induction a <;> constructor <;> assumption

503--- ### Exercise (3 stars): bevalR ⭐⭐⭐
504-
505--- Write a relation `Bexp.EvalR` in the same style as `Aexp.EvalR`, and prove
506--- that it is equivalent to `Bexp.eval`.
507-
508-inductive Bexp.EvalR : Bexp → Bool → Prop where
509-  | bool (b : Bool) : EvalR (.bool b) b
510-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.eq a1 a2) (n1 == n2)
511-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.neq a1 a2) (n1 != n2)
512-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.le a1 a2) (n1 ≤ n2)
513-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.gt a1 a2) (n1 > n2)
514-  | not (b : Bexp) (bv : Bool) (h : EvalR b bv) : EvalR (.not b) (!bv)
515-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp) (tv1 tv2 : Bool) (h1 : EvalR b1 tv1) (h2 : EvalR b2 tv2) :
516-      EvalR (.and b1 b2) (tv1 && tv2)
517-
518-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓b " b:56 => Bexp.EvalR e b
519-
520--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
521---     There is no keyboard shortcut for a subscript b, nor is there one for c
522---     (to use used with cevalR below). There are numbers, x, y, z, l, m, n,
523---     etc.
524-
525-theorem Bexp.evalR_iff_eval (b : Bexp) (bv : Bool) :
526-    b ⇓b bv ↔ b.eval = bv := by
527-  all_goals
528-    constructor
529-    · intro h
530-      induction h <;> simp_all [Aexp.evalR_iff_eval]
531-    · intro h
532-      subst h
533-      induction b <;> constructor <;> simp_all [Aexp.evalR_iff_eval]

535-end Slang
536-
537--- ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
538-
539--- For the definitions of evaluation for arithmetic and boolean expressions,
540--- the choice of whether to use functional or relational definitions is mainly
541--- a matter of taste. However, there are situations where relational
542--- definitions work much better than functional ones.
543-
544-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
545-
546--- For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic operations
547--- with division:
548-
549-inductive Aexp where
550-  | num (n : Nat)
551-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
552-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
553-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
554-  | div (a1 a2 : Aexp)             -- NEW
555-
556--- Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new operation would
557--- not be straightforward due to division being a *partial* operation; i.e.,
558--- what should we return as the result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? By
559--- contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational version of the
560--- definition.
561-
562-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
563-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
564-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
565-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
566-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
567-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
568-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
569-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
570-  | div (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 n3 : Nat)             -- NEW
571-      (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) (hpos : n2 > 0) (hdiv : n2 * n3 = n1) :
572-      EvalR (.div a1 a2) n3
573-
574--- Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of 0) for which
575--- this relation does not specify an output.
576-
577-end Slang.AevalRDivision
578-
579-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
580-
581--- As another example, suppose that we want to extend the arithmetic
582--- operations by a nondeterministic number generator `any` that, when
583--- evaluated, may yield any number. (This is not the same as making a
584--- *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say which results are
585--- *possible*.)
586-
587-inductive Aexp where
588-  | any                            -- NEW
589-  | num (n : Nat)
590-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
591-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
592-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
593-
594--- Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since evaluation is now *not*
595--- a deterministic function from expressions to numbers; but extending the
596--- relation is no problem.
597-
598-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
599-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
600-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
601-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
602-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
603-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
604-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
605-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
606-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
607-
608-end Slang.AevalRExtended
609-
610--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
611---     The following text seems not quite right to me. First, you can use
612---     options for partial functions, and that's very natural to do in Lean as
613---     a monad. Second, and related, monadic functions need not even be
614---     terminating if the implement the `CCPO` typeclass and are labeled as a
615---     `partial_fixpoint`. Maybe we don't want to get into the second thing
616---     here, but failing to mention options (which I think were introduced in
617---     LF) seems a bit surprising.
618-
619--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
620---     Agreed.
621-
622--- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
623--- default?
624-
625--- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function -- or is
626--- genuinely *not* a function -- there is no real choice. When both styles are
627--- workable, relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to
628--- understand, and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles
629--- from them. On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
630--- deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these
631--- if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify
632--- them during proofs.
633-
634--- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
635--- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
636--- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above.
637-
638--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
639---     Well, we didn't actually do a proof that switched between the points of
640---     view. Should we?
641-

21-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
22-declare_syntax_cat invAlt
23-syntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt
24-
25-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
26-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
27-declare_syntax_cat invAlts
28-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
29-
30-/--
31-  `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,
32-  then solves away contradictory generated goals.
33-  `t` itself will also be generalized with a heterogeneous equality `heq`
34-  if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.
35-  * If `inversion +clear t` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
36-    along with `t` if there are no dependencies on it.
37-  * The form `inversion t with | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...` is supported,
38-    similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.
39--/
40-syntax (name := inversion)
41-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (colGe invAlts)+)? : tactic

45-namespace Lean.Meta
46-
47-/--
48-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
49-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
50-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
51-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
52-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
53-
54-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
55-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
56-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
57-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
58-
59-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
60--/
61-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
62-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
63-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
64-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
65-  unless ms.size == 1 do
66-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
67-    else throwError m!"Failed"
68-  let mut mvs := ms
69-  let mut bis := bs
70-  let mut out : Expr := tp
71-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
72-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
73-    unless ms.size == 1 do
74-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
75-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
76-    bis := bis ++ bs
77-    out := tp
78-  return (mvs, bis, out)
79-
80-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
81-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
82-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
83-  return decl.userName
84-
85-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
86-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
87-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
88-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
89-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
90-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
91-
92-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
93-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
94-  match eqs with
95-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
96-  | eq :: eqs =>
97-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
98-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
99-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
100-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
101-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
102-
103-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
104-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
105-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
106-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
107-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
108-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
109-    else return some { s with
110-      mvarId := mvarId,
111-      subst  := subst,
112-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
113-    }
114-
115-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
116-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
117-
118-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
119-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
120-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
121-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
122-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
123-    return { s with mvarId }
124-
125-end Lean.Meta

132-/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
133-macro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)

135-/--
136-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
137-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
138-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
139-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
140-  original `i`.
141-
142-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
143--/
144-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
145-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
146-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
147-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
148-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
149-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
150-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
151-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
152-      catch _ => continue
153-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
154-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
155-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
156-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
157-
158-structure InversionConfig where
159-  clear : Bool := false
160-
161-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
162-
163-open Cases in
164-def inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List CasesSubgoal) := withMainContext do
165-  let goal ← getMainGoal
166-  goal.withContext do
167-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
168-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
169-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
170-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
171-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
172-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
173-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
174-        else pure subgoals
175-      return subgoals.toList
176-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
177-    else
178-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
179-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
180-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
181-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
182-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
183-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
184-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
185-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
186-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
187-        else pure subgoals
188-      return subgoals.toList
189-
190-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
191-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
192-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
193-def evalInvAlt (goals : List CasesSubgoal) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
194-  match alt with
195-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
196-    if let some goal := goals.find? (matchTag tag.getId $ ·.ctorName.getD default) then
197-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal.mvarId]
198-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
199-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
200-    if !goals.isEmpty then
201-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics ·.mvarId)
202-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
203-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
204-where
205-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
206-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
207-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
208-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
209-    unless goals.isEmpty do
210-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
211-    return goal
212-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
213-    let goalMsgs := goals.filterMap (.ofName <$> ·.ctorName)
214-    return if goals.isEmpty
215-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
216-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
217-
218-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
219-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
220-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
221-    let config ← elabInversionConfig config
222-    let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
223-    if let some alts := alts? then
224-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
225-      for alt in expandedAlts do
226-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
227-        goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·.mvarId)
228-      unless goals.isEmpty do
229-        reportUnsolvedGoals $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
230-    replaceMainGoal $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
231-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
232-where expandInvAlts
233-  | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
234-    args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
235-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
236-
237-end Lean.Elab.Tactic
238-
239-end -- meta section

LF/Typeclasses.lean

1-import HL.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Typeclasses
4-
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6--- variable with no constraint on it:
7-
8-variable (α : Type)
9-
10--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
12---     lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13---
14---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15---
16---     Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?
17-
18--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
19---     Yes, in Poly!
20-
21--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
22--- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
23--- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
24--- `a : α`.
25-
26--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
27--- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
28--- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
29--- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
30--- languages, such as traits in Rust.
31-
32--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
33-
34--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
35--- occurs in a list:
36-
37-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
38-  match xs with
39-  | [] => false
40-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
43-
44-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
45-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
46-
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
48-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
49-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
50-
51--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
52--- `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a type
53--- variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
54-
55-sf_expect_failure
56-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
57-    match xs with
58-    | [] => false
59-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
60-
61--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on a
62--- value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one way
63--- to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test to use.
64-
65-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
66-  match xs with
67-  | [] => false
68-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
69-
70-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
71-
72--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
73--- supply, the right equality function.
74-
75--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
76--- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify
77--- something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the needed
78--- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
79--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class, different ones for
80--- different types, are called *instances*. For functions that would use such
81--- instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on the
82--- polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This directs
83--- Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill in the
84--- appropriate instance when the function is called.
85-
86--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
87-
88-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
89-  match xs with
90-  | [] => false
91-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
92-
93-theorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
94-
95-theorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
96-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
97-
98-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
99-
100--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
101--- differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter `eq`,
102--- whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The
103--- instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at
104--- call sites for the particular type `α` that is used. Second, whereas
105--- `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to test equality,
106--- `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when we first used it,
107--- `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
108--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function `Nat.beq`
109--- explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in automatically based on
110--- the type `Nat` of the `List`.
111-
112--- Note to developers (xhalo32):
113---     This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes from
114---     `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of
115---     `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
116---     how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
117-
118--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the instance
119--- implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was fully generic —
120--- so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and
121--- no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
122-
123--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far. We'll
124--- see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how to define
125--- a typeclass in the first place.
126-
127--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
128-
129--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of our
130--- own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis — that made
131--- `==` resolve automatically above.
132-
133--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
134--- defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
135--- `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default value
136--- an explicit parameter:
137-
138-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
139-  match xs with
140-  | [] => defaultValue
141-  | hd :: _ => hd
142-
143-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
144-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
145-
146--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an element
147--- of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based on the type
148--- of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
149-
150--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things. One
151--- is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the caller
152--- always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some information about
153--- what it should search *for*.
154-
155--- Considering the second problem first: The way to provide this information
156--- is to *name* the type-level concept we're after — the **default value** of
157--- a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give
158--- a type-level concept a name; structures can also bundle together more than
159--- one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we only need a
160--- single field here.
161-
162--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
163---     "type-level concept" doesn't say much to me here, and structures are
164---     *not* type-level things. (Well, `structure`s are, but *a* structure
165---     satisfying some `structure` declaration is not, if you see what I
166---     mean...)
167-
168--- Considering the first problem: we need to mark this particular structure as
169--- one Lean should search for automatically — not every `structure`-typed
170--- argument should be.
171-
172--- Let's build up to what wewant in two steps: first the naming, as a plain
173--- `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the
174--- structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
175--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
176-
177-namespace DefaultValueScratch
178-
179-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
180-  value : α
181-
182--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to serve as
183--- the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is, by supplying
184--- a `Nat` for the `value` field:
185-
186-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
187-  value := 1
188-
189-example : natDefault.value = 1 := rfl
190-
191-end DefaultValueScratch
192-
193--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
194---     Maybe the example is not needed?
195-
196--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the sort
197--- of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs to for
198--- `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class`
199--- in place of `structure`:
200-
201-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
202-  value : α
203-
204--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of `def`, we
205--- use `instance`:
206-
207-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
208-  value := 1
209-
210--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
211---     Boldface, or italic? We should write down a rule in STYLE.md!
212-
213--- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via **typeclass synthesis** (or
214--- **typeclass inference**) — the same process that found `BEq Nat` earlier.
215--- That means we can rewrite `List.headOr_ex` the same way we rewrote
216--- `List.elem_poly_eq` into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the explicit
217--- `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
218-
219-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
220-  match xs with
221-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
222-  | hd :: _ => hd
223-
224-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
225-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
226-
227-example : DefaultValue.value = (1 : Nat) := rfl
228-
229--- Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no instance named.
230--- Because the expression equates `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `1`,
231--- Lean selects `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for `DefaultValue Nat`. We
232--- know this because we are able to prove that `DefaultValue.value` is equal
233--- to 1.
234-
235--- Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of integers
236--- `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
237-
238-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
239-  value := -1
240-
241--- Now, Lean can infer instances for both types, including inside
242--- `List.headOr`:
243-
244-example : DefaultValue.value = (1 : Nat) := rfl
245-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
246-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 1 := rfl
247-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := rfl
248-
249--- Synthesis infers instances we could have specified explicitly:
250-
251-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (1 : Nat) := rfl
252-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
253-
254--- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
255-
256-set_option pp.all true in
257-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
258-
259--- @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
260-
261-set_option pp.all true in
262-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
263-
264--- @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
265-
266--- This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt` as the
267--- instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the same search directly:
268-
269-#synth DefaultValue Nat
270-
271--- instDefaultValueNat
272-
273--- For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a term, such as the
274--- `1` above, rather than only proofs (which we will see below) — we expect at
275--- most one instance per type, so this search has a unique answer.
276-
277--- We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library cousin, `Inhabited`, to work
278--- later in this chapter, when we define maps that need a default value for a
279--- generic type. First, though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and see how
280--- its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets resolved.
281-
282--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
283---     Is it a cousin, or a duplicate?
284-
285--- ## Using Typeclasses
286-
287--- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
288--- turned off:
289-
290-set_option pp.notation false in
291-#check 1 == 2
292-
293--- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a field
294--- of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
295-
296--- class BEq (α : Type u) where
297---   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
298---   beq : α → α → Bool
299-
300--- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
301--- type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `DefaultValue` instance
302--- above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
303-
304-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
305-  beq := Nat.beq
306-
307--- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly` is
308--- called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing
309--- `instDefaultValueNat` for `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated
310--- with `(1 : Nat)`.
311-
312--- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
313-
314--- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when specialized to
315--- natural numbers.
316-
317-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
318-  all_goals(
319-  induction xs with
320-  | nil =>
321-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_nil, List.elem_nat_nil]
322-    rfl
323-  | cons hd tl ih =>
324-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_cons, List.elem_nat_cons, ih]
325-    rfl)
326-
327--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
328-
329--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may carry
330--- — any value of the right type will do. But sometimes enforcing constraints
331--- on data is useful. For example, suppose we want to specify that a type has
332--- not just a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
333-
334-sf_experiment
335-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
336-    one : α
337-    two : α
338-
339--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it allows `one` and
340--- `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry
341--- proofs along with data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
342--- and `two` are distinct.
343-
344-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
345-  one : α
346-  two : α
347-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
348-
349--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before, except that now
350--- the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a proof:
351-
352-instance : HasTwo Nat where
353-  one := 1
354-  two := 2
355-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
356-
357--- In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is not possible
358--- to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls to the author
359--- to check, informally, that any required invariants are satisfied, which can
360--- lead to bugs.
361-
362--- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
363-
364--- Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define a class
365--- `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements, and
366--- give an instance of it for `Nat`.
367-
368-class HasThree (α : Type) where
369-  one : α
370-  two : α
371-  three : α
372-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
373-  one_neq_three : one ≠ three
374-  two_neq_three : two ≠ three
375-
376-instance : HasThree Nat where
377-  one := 1
378-  two := 2
379-  three := 3
380-  one_neq_two := (by intro contra; contradiction)
381-  one_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
382-  two_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
383-
384--- ## Maps
385-
386--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
387--- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
388--- them in many places in later volumes.
389-
390--- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a "default"
391--- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
392--- *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate success or
393--- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as
394--- the default element.
395-
396--- ### Key and Value Types
397-
398--- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
399--- into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. Instead of
400--- choosing concrete types for these, we will use type variables.
401-
402--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
403---     Should we perhaps refer back to where the `variable` declaration is
404---     explained? (I guess in Poly, but which section?)
405---
406---     More generally, the exposition gets a little thick from here to the
407---     next section header.
408-
409-variable {α : Type} {β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
410-
411-set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
412-
413--- Here, `α` is the type of the keys and `β` the corresponding values. In
414--- addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, the key type `α` requires
415--- instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
416-
417--- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
418--- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
419---   /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
420---   protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
421-
422--- /--
423--- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
424-
425--- In other words:
426---  * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
427---  * `a == a` is true.
428--- -/
429--- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
430---   /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
431---   eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
432-
433--- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
434--- coincides with proposition equality `=`.
435-
436--- We place no constraints on the value type `β`.
437-
438--- ### Total Maps
439-
440--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`, with
441--- a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we
442--- are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
443--- of this representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view of maps,
444--- as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to
445--- every query in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
446--- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies
447--- proofs that use maps.
448-
449--- Note to developers (Claude):
450---     This paragraph previously wrote `{tech}_extensional_`, but that failed
451---     to build here with `No term def with key "extensional"`. The `{tech}`
452---     role emits a **reference** to a technical term that must resolve to a
453---     matching `{deftech}` definition; the only `{deftech}_extensional_`
454---     lives in the Logic chapter, and Verso's tech-term index isn't shared
455---     with this chapter's build, so the key can't be found. We flattened it
456---     to plain emphasis (`_extensional_`), matching how Logic itself renders
457---     in the generated `.lean`. Alternative fixes if we want a live link: add
458---     a local `{deftech}` for the term in this chapter, or arrange for
459---     cross-chapter `{tech}` references to resolve in a whole-book build.
460-
461-def TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := α → β
462-
463-namespace TotalMap
464-
465--- Intuitively, a total map over an element type `β` is just a function that
466--- can be looked up using a corresponding `a : α`.
467-
468--- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
469--- typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
470--- `DefaultValue` example from above:
471-
472-variable [Inhabited β]
473-
474--- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a default
475--- element; this map always returns the default element when applied to any
476--- key.
477-
478-def empty : TotalMap α β := fun _ ↦ default
479-
480--- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
481--- `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
482--- standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this
483--- empty map.
484-
485-instance : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
486-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
487-
488--- Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to `Nat` values:
489-
490-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
491-
492--- Since a map is a function, we can apply it to a key to get out the
493--- corresponding value, like so:
494-
495-example : emptyNatMap 1 = default := rfl
496-example : emptyNatMap 2 = 0 := rfl
497-
498--- (For `Nat` the `default` is `0`.)
499-
500--- #### Getting Elements
501-
502--- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood, we
503--- would prefer not to expose this fact in their public interface.
504--- Accordingly, we define new operations for querying and updating mappings.
505--- As a first attempt at a query operation, playing the role that `find`
506--- played for the Lists chapter's list-based maps, we could define a function
507--- `getElem` for getting the value associated with a key:
508-
509-sf_experiment
510-  def getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a: α) := m a
511-  
512-  example : getElem emptyNatMap 2 = 0 := rfl
513-
514--- To make element-getting lighter weight, let's define notation so we can
515--- write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than `getElem emptyNatMap`. We could notate
516--- `getElem` directly — we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but here
517--- we'll instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass, `MyGetElem`, and
518--- notate *instances* of it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to
519--- `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for any type with a `MyGetElem` instance, not just
520--- `TotalMap`.
521-
522--- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same
523--- notation is useful for many different types. We have seen the approach
524--- already with `==`: writing `a == b` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by
525--- instance search for whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw
526--- overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation for
527--- `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a simpler
528--- version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which has many
529--- instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to
530--- illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
531-
532-end TotalMap
533-
534--- The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the map
535--- implementation, its keys, and its values.
536-
537-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
538-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
539-
540--- (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to Lean that
541--- helps typeclass inference.)
542-
543--- The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap` is:
544-
545-variable [Inhabited β]
546-instance : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
547-  getElem m a := m a
548-
549--- Now we can associate the bracket syntax with `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've
550--- defined custom notation before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter Lists,
551--- including an `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation lists back
552--- out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with `infixl`/`infixr` or
553--- `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach for the more general
554--- `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting the `m[a]` syntax to work.
555--- (Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules`
556--- and the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities.)
557-
558--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
559---     Can we point people to where they can read about these things if they
560---     are interested?
561-
562-namespace MyGetElem
563-
564-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => `(getElem $xs $i)
565-
566-@[app_unexpander getElem]
567-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
568-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
569-  | _ => throw ()
570-end MyGetElem
571-
572-open scoped MyGetElem
573-
574--- Since the standard library already declares the `$x[$i]` syntax for
575--- `GetElem`, we only need to define the `macro_rules`, not the `notation` as
576--- we have done previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override the
577--- default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when `open scoped MyGetElem` is in
578--- force.
579-
580--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
581---     Make sure we've really explained `open scoped` somewhere...
582-
583--- Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`, we can now use the
584--- notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`.
585-
586-namespace TotalMap
587-
588-theorem getElem_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m a := by rfl
589-
590-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
591-
592--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
593---     As per the discussion in
594---     `https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean/pull/166#discussion_r3690573597`,
595---     we should provide the reverse of `getElem_def` as a simp-lemma, but it
596---     doesn't seem to behave nicely:
597---
598---     `@[simp]
599---     theorem apply_eq_getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by rfl`
600---
601---     The reverse direction of `getElem_def` is provided as a `simp`-lemma.
602---
603---     `example (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m a = m[a] := by
604---       -- simp -- doesn't work (infinite loop)
605---       -- dsimp -- doesn't work (nothing happens)
606---       -- rw [apply_eq_getElem] -- doesn't work: The pattern to be substituted is a metavariable (`?m ?a`) in this equality: ?m ?a = ?m[?a]
607---       rw [apply_eq_getElem m a] -- works`
608---
609---     Explanation of the infinite loop by Yipeng Liu (berberman): To see why,
610---     with `trace.Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite` enabled and specifying maxSteps
611---     to simp, we can track what's going on:
612---
613---     `[Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
614---           m a
615---         ==>
616---           m[a]
617---     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
618---           m[a]
619---         ==>
620---           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
621---     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
622---           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
623---         ==>
624---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
625---     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
626---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
627---         ==>
628---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
629---     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
630---           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
631---         ==>...`
632---
633---     So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too board, causing
634---     this lemma repeating itself. First we have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is
635---     defeq to (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m to be a
636---     TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this lemma applies again --
637---     `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]` which is
638---     `(MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]` and keep going.
639-
640--- #### Updating Elements
641-
642--- Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`, a key `a`, and
643--- a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes every
644--- other key to whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map function
645--- around the old one.
646-
647-def update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β :=
648-  fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
649-
650--- This definition is a nice example of higher-order programming: `update`
651--- takes a function `m` and yields a new function `fun a' => ...` that behaves
652--- like the desired map.
653-
654--- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where `"foo"`
655--- and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped to `false`,
656--- like this:
657-
658-def exampleMap :=
659-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
660-    |>.update "foo" true
661-    |>.update "bar" true
662-
663--- Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means `x.f y`, letting us
664--- chain a sequence of function or method calls left to right without nested
665--- parentheses.
666-
667--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
668---     Should we introduce this notation earlier? (Are there good places to
669---     use it earlier?)
670-
671--- We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time, rather than
672--- going through a typeclass and its own `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as
673--- we did for `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
674--- `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update` doesn't need to work
675--- generically across container types (there's no standard-library operation
676--- like `GetElem` that we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
677--- suffices.
678-
679-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
680-
681-theorem update_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
682-  a →ₜ b ; m = fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := rfl
683-
684--- We can hide the last case when it is empty:
685-
686-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
687-
688--- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
689-
690-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
691-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
692-
693--- This completes the definition of total maps.
694-
695-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := rfl
696-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := rfl
697-
698-example : exampleMap'["baz"] = false := rfl
699-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := rfl
700-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := rfl
701-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := rfl
702-
703--- When we use maps in later volumes, we'll need several fundamental facts
704--- about how they behave.
705-
706--- Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure you thoroughly
707--- understand the statements of the lemmas!
708-
709--- (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality axiom `funext`,
710--- discussed in the Logic chapter.)
711-
712--- First, the empty map returns its default element for all keys:
713-
714-theorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := rfl
715-
716--- Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new value `b` and then
717--- look up `a` in the map resulting from the `update`, we get back `b`:
718-
719-theorem update_eq (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
720-  rw [update_def, getElem_def, ReflBEq.rfl, cond_true]
721-
722--- On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁` and then look up a
723--- *different* key `a₂` in the resulting map, we get the same result that `m`
724--- would have given:
725-
726--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_neq ⭐⭐
727-
728-theorem update_neq {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
729-    (a₁ →ₜ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
730-  all_goals
731-    rw [update_def, getElem_def, beq_false_of_ne h, cond_false]
732-
733--- The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we first need to
734--- say when two maps are equal. Since a total map is implemented as a
735--- function, this is exactly the functional extensionality principle
736--- (`funext`) from the Logic chapter: two maps are equal when they agree at
737--- every key. Recording it once, for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the
738--- `ext` tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the proofs
739--- below.
740-
741-@[ext]
742-theorem ext {m₁ m₂ : TotalMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := funext h
743-
744--- If we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a value `b₁` and then update again
745--- with the same key `a` and another value `b₂`, the resulting map behaves the
746--- same (gives the same result when applied to any key) as the simpler map
747--- obtained by performing just the second `update` on `m`:
748-
749--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_shadow ⭐⭐
750-
751-theorem update_shadow (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
752-    (a →ₜ b₂ ; a →ₜ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₜ b₂ ; m) := by
753-  all_goals
754-    ext a'
755-    by_cases h : a = a'
756-    · subst h
757-      rw [update_eq, update_eq]
758-    · rw [update_neq h, update_neq h, update_neq h]
759-
760--- Given keys `a₁` and `a₂`, the tactic `by_cases` `h : a₁ = a₂` splits the
761--- proof into the case where they are equal — where `subst h` then replaces
762--- one by the other — and the case where they are not, which is what
763--- `update_neq` wants. Use it to prove the following theorem, which states
764--- that if we update a map to assign key `a` the same value as it already has
765--- in `m`, then the result is equal to `m`:
766-
767--- Note to developers (mwhicks1, NOW):
768---     Two things the Rocq source says here have been dropped.
769---
770---     Rocq frames this case analysis around `destruct (eqb_spec x1 x2)`,
771---     which "simultaneously performs case analysis on the result of
772---     `String.eqb x1 x2` and generates hypotheses about the equality (in the
773---     sense of `=`) of `x1` and `x2`" — the boolean/propositional reflection
774---     idiom. The paragraph above replaces that with `by_cases`/`subst`, which
775---     is what the Lean proof uses. But reflection is what the `Reflection`
776---     section **below** is about, so the two may want to be connected rather
777---     than have one silently displace the other.
778---
779---     Rocq then says "With the example in chapter **IndProp** as a template,
780---     use `String.eqb_spec` to prove ...". That cross-reference is dropped,
781---     since it is unclear what the Lean `IndProp` chapter will end up
782---     containing. Revisit later.
783-
784--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_same ⭐⭐
785-
786-theorem update_same (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : (a →ₜ m[a] ; m) = m := by
787-  all_goals
788-    ext a'
789-    by_cases h : a = a'
790-    · subst h
791-      rw [update_eq]
792-    · rw [update_neq h]
793-
794--- Similarly, prove one final property of the `update` function: if we update
795--- a map `m` at two distinct keys, it doesn't matter in which order we do the
796--- updates.
797-
798--- Note to developers (mwhicks1, NOW):
799---     Rocq says "Similarly, use `String.eqb_spec` to prove ..."; the
800---     instruction to use a specific lemma is dropped here for the same reason
801---     as in the note above.
802-
803--- ### Exercise (3 stars): update_permute ⭐⭐⭐
804-
805-theorem update_permute {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} {b₁ b₂ : β} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) :
806-    (a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; m) = (a₂ →ₜ b₂ ; a₁ →ₜ b₁ ; m) := by
807-  all_goals
808-    ext a'
809-    by_cases h₁ : a₁ = a'
810-    · subst h₁
811-      rw [update_eq, update_neq h.symm, update_eq]
812-    · rw [update_neq h₁]
813-      by_cases h₂ : a₂ = a'
814-      · subst h₂
815-        rw [update_eq, update_eq]
816-      · rw [update_neq h₂, update_neq h₂, update_neq h₁]
817-
818--- Note to developers:
819---     The Rocq source also has `getElem_empty` (originally `apply_empty`) and
820---     `update_eq` as (optional) exercises; here they are worked examples,
821---     since `update_eq` was already presented that way. Reconsider if this
822---     section is rebalanced.
823-
824-end TotalMap
825-
826--- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
827-
828--- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation for concrete
829--- maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To accomplish this we define a
830--- simple structure that consists of a key and a value along with `↦` notation
831--- for it.
832-
833-/--
834-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
835--/
836-@[ext]
837-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
838-  key : K
839-  value : V
840-
841-namespace KVPair
842-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
843-end KVPair
844-
845-open scoped KVPair
846-
847--- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances — the standard-library
848--- typeclasses behind the `{x, y, ...}` and `{x}` collection-literal notation
849--- that `List`, `Finset`, and other stdlib containers already support — so
850--- that `TotalMap` can use it too.
851-
852-namespace TotalMap
853-
854-variable [Inhabited β]
855-
856-instance : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
857-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
858-
859-instance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
860-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
861-
862-instance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
863-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
864-
865-end TotalMap
866-
867--- Here are a couple of examples using the new notation:
868-
869-example : ({ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }) = "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅ := rfl
870-
871-example : ({ "foo" ↦ true } : TotalMap String Bool)["foo"] = true := rfl
872-
873-example : ({ 1 ↦ 2, 1 ↦ 3 } : TotalMap Nat Nat)[1] = 2 := rfl
874-
875--- The reason we need to explicitly specify the type of the map is that Lean
876--- doesn't know what type of collection `{ "foo" ↦ true }` is without type

972--- update, we create a new partial map from `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by
973--- wrapping it in angle brackets, i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax.
974--- This is equivalent to writing `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We
975--- also introduce a similar notation for it as for total maps.

1161--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
1162--- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1163-
1164--- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1165-
1166--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1167---     Check formatting:
1168-
1169--- - ⠀
1170--- - `Bool`
1171--- - `Prop`
1172--- - decidable?
1173--- - yes
1174--- - no
1175--- - useable with `match`?
1176--- - yes
1177--- - no
1178--- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1179--- - no
1180--- - yes
1181-
1182--- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1183--- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1184--- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1185--- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1186-
1187--- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1188--- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1189--- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1190--- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1191--- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1192-
1193--- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1194--- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1195--- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1196--- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
1197--- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
1198--- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
1199--- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1200-
1201--- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1202--- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
1203--- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1204--- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1205--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
1206--- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
1207--- or as a function into Prop.
1208-
1209--- As an example, we can write

1212-example : isEven 42 := rfl
1213-
1214--- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1215-
1216-unseal double in
1217-example : Even 42 := by exists 21
1218-
1219--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1220--- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1221-

1408--- of choice to provide a proof that all propositions are *classically*
1409--- decidable. This sort of definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is
1410--- not allowed to be used in conjunction with computational features of Lean
1411--- such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval` command.
